source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Blind expert review of research ideas on 7 NLP topics. LLM-generated ideas were rated more novel than ideas written by human experts. Feasibility was not significantly different.
numbers: 49 ideas per condition. Novelty mean: human 4.84 (SD 1.79), AI 5.64 (SD 1.76), AI + human rerank 5.81 (SD 1.66), 1-10 scale, Welch t-tests with Bonferroni, p<0.01. 79 reviewers, 49 idea writers.
limits: Ideas only, never executed. Human ideas were written under a time limit by experts who may not have submitted their best idea. Three different statistical tests were used to guard against reviewer and topic confounds.
agent_relevance: Novelty gains on an LLM-picked question are real in the eyes of reviewers, but see b05 for what happens after execution. Do not treat judged novelty as a pass signal for S0.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: LLM idea generation collapses into duplicates. Large-scale sampling does not give a large set of distinct questions.
numbers: 4000 seed ideas per topic pool: only about 5% (about 200) were non-duplicates at cosine similarity 0.8 (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). The share of new non-duplicates falls with each batch and the accumulated count plateaus.
limits: Duplicate test is an embedding threshold of 0.8, set by manual inspection. Result depends on the generation prompt and topic.
agent_relevance: When the agent lists candidate questions at S0, sample count is not diversity. Dedupe by a code check and expect a plateau.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Reviewers of ideas disagree a lot. Agreement among humans is low, and LLM judges are worse than humans at ranking ideas.
numbers: Inter-reviewer balanced accuracy 56.1% (random 50%). NeurIPS 2021 consistency experiment 66.0%. ICLR 2024 LM submissions 71.9%. Best LLM judge (Claude-3.5 pairwise ranker) 53.3%.
limits: Idea-stage review is more subjective than paper review, the authors say. Agreement metric is top vs bottom 25% on split-half reviewers.
agent_relevance: An LLM judging question quality is near chance. Do not let the model grade which problem to pick. Use code checks.

source: Si, Yang, Hashimoto (2024) Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A large-scale human study with 100+ NLP researchers
finding: Reviewers' overall score follows novelty and excitement and ignores feasibility.
numbers: Correlation of overall score with novelty r=0.725, excitement r=0.854, feasibility r<0.1.
limits: Correlation inside one reviewer pool of NLP experts. Says what reviewers reward, not what produces good research.
agent_relevance: Human taste for questions overweights novelty. A selector built on this taste would inherit that bias and the later drop (b05).

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Follow-up that ran the ideas. 43 experts each spent over 100 hours executing a randomly assigned idea (human or LLM). Before execution LLM ideas won on all metrics. After execution the ranking flipped.
numbers: Ideation scores AI vs human: novelty 5.78 vs 4.91, excitement 5.65 vs 4.40, effectiveness 6.00 vs 4.83, overall 5.38 vs 4.60 (FDR p 0.001-0.035). After execution: novelty 4.73 vs 4.90, excitement 3.90 vs 4.48, effectiveness 4.13 vs 4.78, overall 3.41 vs 3.97, none significant. N=19 human ideas, N=24 AI ideas. 58 blind reviewers.
limits: Small N. The post-execution ranking flip is not significant when each idea is one data point. Execution was in NLP topics only. The significant result is the drop within idea, not the flip.
agent_relevance: Strongest evidence against picking a problem by how novel it looks. S0 should test whether the question can be carried out and checked, not only whether it sounds new.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Within-idea change from ideation to execution: LLM ideas lost much more than human ideas.
numbers: Mean change after execution, human ideas: novelty -0.010, excitement +0.078, effectiveness -0.052, overall -0.628. AI ideas: novelty -1.049, excitement -1.760, effectiveness -1.879, overall -1.976 (1-10 scale). Difference significant on all four: p 0.025, 0.001, 0.003, 0.004 (FDR).
limits: Reviewers differed between stages, and each idea had few executors. Gap controls for idea quality but not for who executed.
agent_relevance: Judged quality of a question before work is a weak predictor of outcome. Prefer a cheap pilot execution before committing.

source: Si, Hashimoto, Yang (2025) The Ideation-Execution Gap: Execution Outcomes of LLM-Generated versus Human Research Ideas
finding: Ideation scores barely predict execution scores. For AI ideas the link is even negative on excitement.
numbers: Pearson r between ideation and execution score. AI ideas: novelty -0.019, excitement -0.321, effectiveness 0.172, overall -0.092. Human ideas: novelty -0.084, excitement 0.205, effectiveness 0.022, overall 0.158.
limits: Correlations on 19 and 24 ideas, so wide uncertainty. No significance claimed.
agent_relevance: Do not train or tune a problem selector on pre-execution human ratings alone.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and Innovation in Scientists' Research Strategies
finding: Biomedical chemistry papers 1983-2008 coded by how they choose chemical relationships: jump, new consolidation, new bridge, repeat consolidation, repeat bridge. Most work repeats known links, and the share of repeating grows over time.
numbers: MEDLINE network by 2008: 181,078 nodes, 84,709,977 links. New or jump statements 14.2% vs repeat 85.8%. Jumps 1.8% vs new bridges plus consolidations 12.4%. Model fit to data Pearson R=0.983.
limits: Observational. Chemicals as the unit of a question; only biomedical chemistry. Whether a link is new depends on MEDLINE indexing.
agent_relevance: Scientists choose conservatively. A default LLM scaffold that copies the literature will inherit this skew toward already-known links.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and Innovation in Scientists' Research Strategies
finding: Rare strategies earn more citations on average but with more spread. This supports the essential-tension view (risk vs reward).
numbers: Strategy surprisal explains 29.2% of variance in mean citations (R2=0.2916, 1983-2002); a 10-fold rarer strategy gives 2.26 more citations on average. Surprisal explains 28.6% of the variance in the standard deviation of citations. Year alone R2=0.52; year plus surprisal R2=0.76.
limits: Aggregate by strategy-year (100 points), not per paper. Citation counts are a proxy for importance.
agent_relevance: Expected value of a bold question is higher, but the downside is wider. A decision rule at S0 needs a risk budget.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and Innovation in Scientists' Research Strategies
finding: Reward by citations is too small to pay for the risk. Only extraordinary rewards (top-cited papers, prizes) show enrichment of risky strategies.
numbers: Break-even argument: for new or jump work to be rational, it would need only 24% (new) or 35% (jump) lower success odds than repeat work, which the authors find implausible. Prize analysis: 137 prizes, 7594 awardees, 241,176 articles.
limits: Success probabilities are not observed; the argument is an inference. Prize winners may differ in other ways.
agent_relevance: Incentive structure explains conservative selection. A scaffold has no career risk, so it can afford the bold picks that humans avoid.

source: Foster, Rzhetsky, Evans (2015) Tradition and Innovation in Scientists' Research Strategies
finding: Strategy mix is unrelated to the opportunities available. The network gets bigger, and scientists shift toward local, repeat work, not toward the new options.
numbers: Largest cluster share of the network fell from 27.5% (1983) to 12.8% (2008). Distinct chemicals in MEDLINE grew 10-fold from 1980 to 2008. Preference for repeating known links rises sharply in the fitted model.
limits: One database and a stylised agent model.
agent_relevance: Problem choice is driven by habit, not by what is possible. Add an explicit step that looks for unexplored neighbours.

source: Rzhetsky, Foster, Foster, Evans (2015) Choosing experiments to accelerate collective discovery (PNAS)
finding: Companion model of the same data: scientists explore close to central molecules; simulations say risk-taking and publishing failures would speed discovery, especially in mature fields.
numbers: Only the abstract and significance text were retrieved (millions of articles, 30 years). No figures or ratios were read.
limits: Body text not opened, so no exact efficiency ratios are recorded. Simulation on a sample network.
agent_relevance: Marks the efficiency gap between observed and best strategies, but the number must be read from the paper before use.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science: a cautionary tale for users of bibliometric indicators (Research Policy)
finding: Novelty measured as first-time combinations of cited journals. Novel papers are rare, high variance, and win in the long run.
numbers: Web of Science articles from 2001, 15-year window. 89% of papers make no new journal combination, 11% make some, 54% of those make exactly one. Citation dispersion 18% higher for highly novel papers. Odds of top 10% vs middle 80%: +18%. Odds of lowest 10%: +15%. Odds of top 1% big hit: +57% for highly novel, +13% for moderately novel.
limits: Novelty is one definition (journal combinations). One cohort year. Field differences handled by subject-category ranks.
agent_relevance: Novel questions pay later and unevenly. A scaffold that scores by quick feedback will undervalue them.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science: a cautionary tale for users of bibliometric indicators (Research Policy)
finding: Delayed recognition: novel papers look worse with short citation windows.
numbers: Highly novel papers are less likely to be top cited if the window is under 3 years, and more likely from year 4. Moderately novel papers need at least 5 years to catch up (significant gain at 9 or more years).
limits: Window analysis for one cohort.
agent_relevance: Short-horizon checks bias against bold problems. Held-out checks should be matched to the horizon of the question.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science: a cautionary tale for users of bibliometric indicators (Research Policy)
finding: Novel papers appear in lower-impact-factor journals, controlling for field.
numbers: Journal Impact Factor is about 10% lower for moderately novel and 17% lower for highly novel papers (Poisson, controls).
limits: The cause (referee bias vs journal strategy vs author choice) is not separated. Not due to new journals.
agent_relevance: Venue prestige is not a reliable stand-in for question value.

source: Wang, Veugelers, Stephan (2017) Bias against novelty in science: a cautionary tale for users of bibliometric indicators (Research Policy)
finding: Novel research is cited across more fields and farther from home.
numbers: Highly novel papers cited by 19% more subject categories, moderately novel 11% more (Poisson). Odds of being cited by big hits +26% (highly novel) and +6% (moderately novel).
limits: Citation-based.
agent_relevance: Bold questions have wider reach, a case for crossing fields when selecting.

source: Packalen, Bhattacharya (2020) NIH funding and the pursuit of edge science (PNAS)
finding: Edge science (building on very recent ideas) is NIH funded less often than work built on ideas 10-25 years old, so funders favour ideas that have matured.
numbers: More than 24 million MEDLINE articles; UMLS terms (over 5 million) give idea vintage. NIH funding rate over 60% for contributions using 10-25 year old ideas, about 50% for very recent or only well-established ideas. 46% of US 2010s papers report NIH funding.
limits: Papers reflect both funder choices and the applications received. The tendency exists mostly in basic science, not clinical.
agent_relevance: A funding or review filter shifts picks toward safe but not stale. Models trained on funded literature copy this.

source: Packalen, Bhattacharya (2020) NIH funding and the pursuit of edge science (PNAS)
finding: The NIH tendency to fund papers built on the newest ideas declined over time. Novel work is funded more because of area composition, not within-area choice.
numbers: Findings: funding gap with delay of about 7 years; limited to basic science; decline over time (no single figure retrieved).
limits: No causal design; abstract-level numbers only for the trend.
agent_relevance: Time-trend evidence that selection is getting more conservative, in line with b08.

source: Hill, Yin, Stein, Wang, Jones, Wang (2025) The pivot penalty in research (Nature)
finding: The further a researcher moves from their own earlier work, the lower the chance of a high-impact result. This is a cost of changing the question.
numbers: 25.8 million papers 1970-2015, 154 fields. Hit = top 5% of citations. Lowest-pivot work hit 7.4% (48% above baseline); highest-pivot 2.2% (56% below). Within the same author: lowest pivot 2.1% more likely, highest 1.8% less likely to be a hit.
limits: The measure uses own prior work as reference. Holds across fields, but cause is unclear (reputation, audience, expertise).
agent_relevance: Switching problem costs a lot. A scaffold with no career identity pays no reputation penalty, but may still lack local expertise.

source: Hill, Yin, Stein, Wang, Jones, Wang (2025) The pivot penalty in research (Nature)
finding: The pivot penalty is nearly universal and growing, and shows up in patents.
numbers: Held in 93% of 154 subfields; grew over time in 88% of fields. Patents 1980-2015, 127 classes: lowest-pivot hit 8.0%, highest-pivot 3.8% (24% below baseline); held in 91% of classes. Top 1% and 0.1% by citations: lowest pivot decile over-represented by 65% and 91%, highest decile under-represented by 69% and 73%.
limits: Cross-sectional associations with controls; not randomised.
agent_relevance: Robust descriptive regularity, likely partly selection. Treat as a base-rate prior for changing questions.

source: Hill, Yin, Stein, Wang, Jones, Wang (2025) The pivot penalty in research (Nature)
finding: The pivot penalty appears in downstream outcomes and persists after exogenous shocks such as retractions or COVID-19.
numbers: Patent citation of high-pivot articles down 43%; publication of high-pivot preprints down 35%; market value of patented inventions down 29%. COVID-19 papers: hit rate fell 61% (COVID) and 59% (non-COVID) from lowest to highest pivot bin. Penalty about 26% less steep when staying in the same journal.
limits: Natural experiments cover push (retraction) and pull (COVID) events only.
agent_relevance: Even when the field makes a strong case for moving, pivoting still costs. Plan for ramp-up.

source: Hill, Yin, Stein, Wang, Jones, Wang (2025) The pivot penalty in research (Nature)
finding: Pivot mechanisms: high-pivot work is more novel in the tail but less conventional, and is less often built on or published.
numbers: 31% of the lowest-pivot vigintile of papers had high tail novelty vs 49-58% in high-pivot vigintiles; 79% of lowest-pivot papers had high median conventionality vs 27-30% in high-pivot.
limits: Novelty metrics are text and citation based.
agent_relevance: Bold pivots are both novel and less anchored. They need bridging steps to be accepted.

source: Gu, Krenn (2024, v4 2026) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 Research Group Leaders
finding: Largest expert evaluation of AI research ideas so far: 110 Max Planck group leaders rated 4,451 personalised ideas (GPT-4 plus knowledge graph). Average interest was low.
numbers: Mean 2.40 on 1-5 (SE 0.02); most common rating 1 (1,632 ideas, 36.7%); 24.9% rated 4 or 5 (394 rated 5). 267 invited, 110 took part (41.2%), 84.3% completion.
limits: Interest is not impact. Raters judged a short suggestion personalised to them. Participants opted in.
agent_relevance: Quality bar for open-ended LLM question generation: about 1 in 4 is judged worth a thought.

source: Gu, Krenn (2024, v4 2026) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 Research Group Leaders
finding: Choosing concept pairs by predicted citation impact does not improve expert-rated interest over a titles-only baseline.
numbers: Mean interest: high-citation-predicted pairs 2.350 (SE 0.034), random pairs 2.446 (SE 0.035), titles-only GPT baseline 2.414 (SE 0.036). The abstract notes a weak lean toward lower interest for high-citation-predicted pairs.
limits: Differences are small. Interest only, no execution.
agent_relevance: Citation-based selectors are not a proxy for what experts find interesting. A failed method for choosing questions.

source: Gu, Krenn (2024, v4 2026) Generating Interesting Scientific Ideas using Knowledge Graphs and LLMs: Evaluations with 100 Research Group Leaders
finding: Graph features predict interest: more connected concepts and more distant researchers lead to less interest.
numbers: Binned slopes: vertex degree k=-0.213 (Spearman -0.166), PageRank k=-0.192 (-0.176), total citations k=-0.143 (-0.153), semantic distance between evaluator and idea k=-0.309 (R2 0.734, Spearman -0.223). v4 compares humans, GPT-4, GPT-5.2 on six evaluators: ratings 4-5 for 29.1% human (n=148), 25.0% GPT-4 (n=100), 32.5% GPT-5.2 (n=160).
limits: Subset comparison is small (six evaluators). Ideas are personalised to the rater.
agent_relevance: Less crowded concepts give more interesting ideas; current LLM ideas are about on par with PhD-student ideas in this narrow test.

source: Sourati, Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Models that include who the experts are (author hypergraph) predict future discoveries better than content-only models. They predict what humans will pick next.
numbers: Up to 400% higher precision. Materials: about 100% higher precision than a word2vec content-only baseline. Drug-disease (CTD, prediction year 2001, 18 years later): 43% higher precision. COVID-19 therapies: 36-38% of predictions entered clinical trials within 12 months and 42% by July 2021 vs 10% and 12% for content-only (350-400% higher).
limits: Retrospective; ground truth is what scientists later did. Works best where the literature is frequently mentioned (r=0.74 with drug frequency).
agent_relevance: Predicting the crowd's next question is feasible, so a scaffold can also compute the opposite: the questions the crowd will not ask.

source: Sourati, Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Tuning the same model to avoid the crowd gives alien hypotheses that humans take much longer to find, and sometimes never within the window.
numbers: Discovery wait times rise as the avoid-the-crowd parameter rises, for most energy properties and 70% of human diseases. For COVID-19 none of the strongly complementary predictions were discovered within the window.
limits: Not shown that alien hypotheses are valuable; the claim is only that they are not found quickly.
agent_relevance: Gives a lever for S0: a distance-from-crowd parameter. Needs a validation check before use.

source: Sourati, Evans (2023) Accelerating science with human-aware artificial intelligence (Nature Human Behaviour)
finding: Dropping author information hurts: removing authors cut precision for materials.
numbers: Precision with vs without authors: 62%, 58%, 74% vs 48%, 50%, 58% for thermoelectricity, ferroelectricity, photovoltaics. 40% of top 50 predicted authors became actual discoverers a year later for thermoelectric and ferroelectric materials.
limits: Methods-section numbers; one domain family.
agent_relevance: Selection is social: who works on what matters as much as content.

source: Krenn et al. (2022) Predicting the Future of AI with AI: high-quality link prediction in an exponentially growing knowledge network (Science4Cast)
finding: Benchmark of predicting which concept pairs in AI literature will be linked. Hand-crafted network features beat pure ML.
numbers: New-link AUC up to 93%. Links formed at least three times reached AUC above 99%. Only about 1-3% of new connections are positive samples. Pure ML did not beat hand-crafted features.
limits: Link formation is a weak proxy for important questions. Authors checked for leakage.
agent_relevance: Predicts what will be asked, which is the crowd's next question. Useful as a novelty baseline, not a value signal.

source: Luo et al. (2024) Large language models surpass human experts in predicting neuroscience results (BrainBench)
finding: LLMs beat experts at predicting which of two versions of an abstract's result is true. Relevant to judging which question is likely to give a clear answer.
numbers: LLMs average 81.4% vs human experts 63.4% (171 of 202 participants passed checks); top-20% self-rated expertise 66.2%. Chat-tuned models worse than base (t(5)=5.4, p=.002).
limits: Backward-looking benchmark of result plausibility, not problem selection.
agent_relevance: LLMs guess likely outcomes well, so a cheap predict-the-result check may help the S0 gate: if the model is sure of the result, the question may add little. Untested idea.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist (Google)
finding: Multi-agent hypothesis generator with Elo tournament ranking. Self-rated Elo rises with compute and tracks correctness on GPQA diamond.
numbers: 203 research goals; Co-Scientist average expert preference rank 2.36, novelty 3.64 and impact 3.09 out of 5 on 11 expert goals. Top-1 GPQA accuracy 78.4% when picking the top-Elo result.
limits: Subjective expert scores from small sets (11 and 15 goals). Elo is LLM-judged, and the authors say expert preferences are not objective ground truth. Developer-run evaluation.
agent_relevance: Tournament selection can separate good from bad answers when a known answer exists; it has not been shown for choosing questions.

source: Gottweis et al. (2025) Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist (Google)
finding: A novelty judge needs retrieval. Without search the judge calls known ideas novel.
numbers: On a set of already-published ideas, novelty score 6.14/10 without search vs 2.38/10 with search. Correctness score 7.4 to 8.46 with search.
limits: Small known-idea set.
agent_relevance: The novelty check at S0 must run against retrieved literature in code, never the model's memory.

source: Lu et al. (2024) The AI Scientist: towards fully automated open-ended scientific discovery
finding: AI Scientist picks its own ideas, scores them for interest, novelty and feasibility, and checks novelty via Semantic Scholar. The scores are self-assessed by the same model.
numbers: About 50 ideas per run seeded with 1-2 examples, about 12 hours on 8 H100s. Automated reviewer scores of selected papers 3-5 (average accepted NeurIPS paper about 6). Novelty search up to 10 rounds.
limits: Authors admit self-assessed novelty makes comparisons across models hard. Selected papers are chosen examples. Self-rating over-estimates.
agent_relevance: Shows the pattern the schema forbids: the model grades its own picks. Self-agreed scores are unreliable (see b03 and b32).

source: Wang et al. (2023) SciMON: Scientific Inspiration Machines Optimized for Novelty
finding: Early test of literature-based idea generation with iterative novelty boosting against retrieved prior work. GPT-4 alone gave ideas with low technical depth and novelty.
numbers: Abstract-level claim only; human evaluation tables were not extracted. Data filter pipeline: instances pass all steps 79.7%.
limits: Only the introduction and method sections were skimmed; no exact novelty numbers recorded. Annotators were six NLP experts.
agent_relevance: Supports retrieval-based novelty loops, but the size of the gain is unverified here.
